title: Study Abroad Report: Johns Hopkins University
paragraphs: My dream is to become a neurologist who leads the world in both clinical practice and research. Partly because my parents work in healthcare, I have seen many patients with neurodegenerative diseases since I was small. Many of them develop the disease relatively young, receive a diagnosis, and are told that with current medicine it will lead to death in a dozen or so years. And as their physical function gradually declines, they are forced to live in constant fear of death. I wanted to support them by removing their spiritual and psychological anxiety, and I aspired to become a doctor. And I felt that I wanted to find treatments for them through research. Since that day, I have spent my student years thinking about what I can do now in order to become a doctor who leads the world in both clinical practice and research. The reason I applied to the study abroad program this time was also to explore what career plans exist for achieving that life goal. I thought I would go and learn how I should be involved in clinical practice and research in the United States in order best to achieve my goal.

In this clerkship, I rotated through cardiology, anesthesiology, and allergy and rheumatology at Johns Hopkins University, and I did basic medical research on Alzheimer's disease at Massachusetts General Hospital.

First, in the cardiology clerkship, I strongly felt the affinity between clinical research and treatment in American medicine. When I presented the treatment plan of my assigned patient to a senior physician, I was criticized that merely showing, for example, the AHA guidelines as the basis for the treatment lacked evidence. I was required to go back to the clinical study that underlies the guideline, consider the subject group in that study, the group excluded from it, and the method of analyzing the treatment effect, and then judge whether my patient was indicated for that treatment. Since I was required to present a paper at the 7 a.m. rounds every day, I went to the ward at about 5 a.m., took the patient's findings and searched for papers, so I think the clerkship placed a greater burden on students than in Japan. However, through this clerkship I acquired the habit of not choosing treatment manually once a diagnosis is made, but going back to the clinical study that is its basis, understanding the design of that study and then considering whether the patient is indicated, and I think that has become an asset for my future.

Also, through the clerkship in anesthesiology, I learned the whole flow of surgery in the United States, which is completely different from Japan. In the United States, most operations are done as same-day surgery or with a one-day hospital stay. Compared with Japan, where hospital stays are long, what is done "in the outpatient clinic" and what is done "during hospitalization" inevitably differ greatly. I trained in preoperative assessment in the outpatient clinic, intraoperative patient management and postoperative pain management in the outpatient clinic. Because preoperative and perioperative management is done in the outpatient setting, it was necessary not only to assess the "current" condition but also to educate about "future changes." In addition to evaluating whether surgery was indicated from physical findings, imaging findings and blood findings, I educated patients about how to respond to symptoms after discharge (pain, suppuration of the surgical wound, preoperative symptoms not remitting, and so on). During surgery, whenever the vital signs changed, I was asked by the senior physician to explain physiologically and pharmacologically what was happening inside the patient's body, and I was able to acquire knowledge of basic medicine. Overall, by coming into contact with a style of surgical treatment different from Japan's, I became able to see the Japanese style objectively.

Finally, the allergy and rheumatology department. In this department I was basically entrusted with taking histories in the outpatient clinic. Although the clerkship period was short, two weeks, I was able to learn many differences from Japan. In the United States there are many kinds of drugs that can be bought at a pharmacy without a prescription. Even drugs with relatively strong effects and strong side effects can be bought without being examined by a doctor. As a result, many patients visit for drug allergies, and a clinic was set up for drug allergy alone. In my clinic I saw patients with drug allergy, food allergy, rhinitis, sinusitis and dermatitis. In the examinations I emphasized above all the viewpoint of whether there was a possibility of anaphylactic shock.

After 13 weeks of clerkship at JHU, I did basic medical research on Alzheimer's disease at MGH. There I removed the cerebral cortex of mouse embryos, cultured neurons, observed their axonal growth using a special device, and analyzed its speed and direction. Compared with laboratories in Japan, it had extremely abundant facilities.

Through this study abroad, I reflected on American medicine and thought about what career I actually want to follow. First, regarding clinical practice in the United States, my impression was that because the authority of other healthcare professionals is large, a complete shift system is adopted and there are many doctors, senior physicians can concentrate on research in their own specialty. Compared with the Japanese attending system, the doctors' quality of life seemed far higher. However, my goal is to be a doctor who can give psychological support to patients with intractable diseases, and in that respect the Japanese attending system, in which the doctor and patient are in a one-to-one relationship and can understand the patient better, seemed attractive. As for research, though, the United States was overwhelmingly better off as an environment. Not only were research funds plentiful, but networks between university hospitals were established and the system for sharing specimen samples was solid. I now think I would like to have the opportunity to do research in the United States after properly undergoing clinical training in Japan.

Finally, I conclude my study abroad report by expressing my deep gratitude to the doctors of the International Exchange Office and the staff of the Academic Affairs Division who supported me in gaining the valuable experience of studying abroad.
